what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Is Meta's crawling clause legal? The law that could reach it, the precedents against Meta, and Meta's own terms the other way round.
sections.para: Meta's updated terms make crawling, caching and test credentials on a business's websites the price of any business use of its products. Not legal advice, and not yet ruled on: but EU and UK law forbid a dominant firm from imposing unconnected obligations, Meta was fined for unfair business terms in 2024, and Meta forbids the same acts on its own products.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Nine lines: not advice, the law's word, Meta's record, the DMA, the UK, copyright, the asymmetry, fines, and the view.
sections.para: Nobody has ruled on the clause. Article 102 and the UK's section 18 name what it does. Meta lost a similar case in 2024. The DMA's fair-access rule is untested; the UK cannot use its new powers. A signed licence can sidestep copyright opt-outs. Meta forbids on its products what it asks of yours. If legal, it should not be.

sections.label: My first reaction
sections.line: Blackmail is the feeling; the law's word is obligations with no connection to the contract, imposed by a dominant firm.
sections.para: My first reaction was that this is blackmail: use a platform for one thing, then give up rights over your website or leave. The law's term is close: Article 102 and the UK's Competition Act forbid a dominant firm from making contracts conditional on supplementary obligations with no connection to their subject, and unfair trading conditions.

sections.label: What the clause actually reaches
sections.line: Not only your website, every business use including WhatsApp, and robots.txt nowhere in the text.
sections.para: The clause covers URLs associated with a business or shared through Meta's products by anyone, applies to every business use of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, and does not mention robots.txt; Meta's own documentation says two of its crawlers may bypass it. 'Train' was removed and the date moved, but publishers say that excludes nothing.

sections.label: The asymmetry
sections.line: Could a publisher do the same to Facebook? Meta's own terms, robots.txt and lawsuits say no.
sections.para: Facebook's terms forbid automated collection without permission; Meta's data collection terms require written permission and obedience to its robots.txt, which blocks AI crawlers and ends with Disallow. WhatsApp forbids automated accounts. Meta sued Voyager Labs for scraping with fake accounts. Courts let logged-off scraping of public pages; the clause goes further, with consent under pressure.

sections.label: The law that could reach it
sections.line: Article 102 and Meta's 2024 fine, Germany's case, the DMA, the P2B rules, the UK's gap, and India's precedent.
sections.para: The Commission fined Meta €797.72 million in 2024 for unfair terms that used business customers' data, and ordered WhatsApp interim measures in 2026. Germany's 2019 case is final. DMA Article 6(12) requires fair access for business users of Facebook and Instagram, untested. P2B rules cover notice. The UK has not designated Meta. India found 'take-it-or-leave-it' terms unfair.

sections.label: The quiet part: copyright
sections.line: A licence the publisher signs can make its machine-readable opt-out irrelevant; a business can only license what it owns.
sections.para: EU law lets text and data mining proceed unless rightholders reserve it machine-readably, but that protects against the exception, not against a licence the publisher signs; the Directive does not protect this exception from contracts. Limits: a business cannot license wire copy or freelance work, the AI Act requires respecting opt-outs, and the UK has no commercial exception.

sections.label: Test credentials, and the people on the page
sections.line: Readers' data on the page, consent under computer misuse law, paywalls, and the Cambridge Analytica question.
sections.para: A logged-in crawler reaches readers' comments and profiles; the publisher cannot consent for them, and Meta was fined €265 million for failing to stop scraping. Consent decides computer misuse, but the account holder may not control the site, and paywall accounts may exceed it. Cambridge Analytica asked who agreed for the people affected; the same question applies.

sections.label: If we get sued, we pay the fine
sections.line: Meta earned about $166 million a day in 2025; its fines have not changed the pattern.
sections.para: The largest GDPR fine, €1.2 billion, is under appeal; the Marketplace fine was €797.72 million and the DMA fine €200 million. Meta's 2025 net income was $60.5 billion. Doctorow: companies that fear a fine larger than the gain will cheat less. The suspicion that Meta has priced this in is a suspicion, but the numbers make it reasonable.

sections.label: A textbook case of enshittification
sections.line: Doctorow's third stage: abuse business customers to claw back value, made possible by switching costs.
sections.para: Facebook is used by 43% for news weekly, and social and video now beat TV and publishers' own sites as sources, while Facebook referrals to news fell 43% in two and a half years. Meta blocked news in Canada rather than pay. The closest analogy is the Commission's Google probe: content as the price of a platform publishers cannot leave.

sections.label: My view: if it is legal, it should not be
sections.line: If it is legal it should not be: a platform should not impose terms it would not accept, and publishers should not wait.
sections.para: The principle: a platform should not impose on business users terms it would not accept from them. Fair would mean no condition without a connection, robots.txt and machine-readable licences binding in the contract, no test credentials, messaging services out, and saying no without losing the tools. Publishers can publish their own machine-readable terms today.

sections.label: What to watch
sections.line: Before 20 November: formal proceedings, the text, a UK designation, the complaints, and the appeals.
sections.para: Watch whether the Commission or the CMA opens formal proceedings, which interim measures need; whether Meta writes robots.txt or a news exclusion into the text; whether the CMA starts a strategic market status investigation; what the complaints argue when published; and the appeals of New Mexico's order and the Marketplace fine.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Not legal advice; dominance not proven here; the copyright point is a reading; some sources are press reports.
sections.para: This is a reading of public texts, not legal advice, and nothing is settled until a regulator or court rules. Article 102 and section 18 need dominance in the relevant market. The copyright point is the author's reading. The complaints are not public, and some facts rest on press reports. Statements are attributed to Meta; the final text may change.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Meta's terms and rules, EU and UK legislation, Commission and German decisions, court cases, Doctorow, and the Reuters Institute.
sections.para: Meta's Commercial Terms preview, Facebook and WhatsApp terms, Automated Data Collection Terms, robots.txt and crawler documentation; Article 102, the Competition Act, the DMA, P2B Regulation, DSM Directive, Computer Misuse Act and DMCC Act; Commission, Bundeskartellamt, CJEU and Irish DPC decisions; Voyager Labs, Bright Data, Cambridge Analytica and New Mexico; Press Gazette, WAN-IFRA, Doctorow, the Reuters Institute.
